aspectTitle: Layout tables that falsely assert data-table relationships: th, caption, scope, or summary on a positioning-only table (F46)
aspectDescription: A table used purely to position page regions (nav | content | sidebar, or a hero/marketing layout) includes data-table semantic markup — a <th>, a <caption>, scope attributes, role=table, or a non-empty summary — which falsely tells AT that the layout grid is meaningful tabular data and that, e.g., 'Page Title' is the header for the nav/content/footer cells. The inverse of the suppression case: here genuine semantic markup is present and syntactically valid, but the relationship it asserts does not exist. Judging this requires recognizing the table is layout (no real row/column data relationsh
scenario: County government 'Records & Licensing Portal' positions its entire page chrome (masthead, left services nav, main content with a record-order form, right office-hours sidebar, footer) in a single layout <table>. The top row is a <th colspan=3 scope=colgroup>Northbridge County</th>, falsely asserting that the agency name is the column header governing the nav/content/sidebar cells beneath it.
mechanism: A <th colspan=3 scope=colgroup> on a layout table designates the agency-name cell as the column header for the page-region cells. AT in table-reading mode announces 'Northbridge County Records & Licensing Portal' as the header that classifies the navigation links, the order form, and the office hours — a relationship that does not exist (these are independent page regions, not data observations sharing a header). F46: a <th> in a layout table is structural markup used purely for presentation.

aspectTitle: Valid structural elements asserting relationships that do not exist: heading/blockquote/fieldset used for visual effect (F43)
aspectDescription: Genuine structural elements are present and syntactically valid, but they assert a content relationship that is false. An <h3>/<h4> makes an author byline or address big and bold (no new section begins), a <blockquote> wraps text that is not a quotation merely to indent it, or a <fieldset>/<legend> draws a decorative bordered box around prose that is not a group of form controls. Automated tools see a well-formed heading/blockquote/fieldset and pass; only a human reading the content can tell the asserted relationship is untrue. This is the Trusted Tester note 'don't use heading markup for emph
scenario: Long-form news article: the byline ("By Marguerite Adler and Tomas Vance") is marked up as <h3> and the dateline as <h4>, between the <h1> title and the real <h2> sections, purely to size them. The byline/date begin no section, fabricating a heading outline (h1 > h3 > h4 > h2) that asserts subsection relationships absent from the content.
mechanism: Screen-reader heading navigation (H key / rotor) announces the byline as a level-3 section and the dateline as a level-4 subsection nested under the title; landing on each, the user finds only author names / a date — no section. Headings assert sectioning relationships (F43) that do not exist; the real first section 'Abstract' is announced after a spurious h3/h4, corrupting the outline.

aspectTitle: Tabular or multi-column information faked with whitespace, line breaks, or <pre> instead of real structure (F34, F48, F33)
aspectDescription: Tabular or multi-column content is laid out using only spaces, tabs, line breaks, or a monospaced <pre> block, so it looks like a table or two parallel columns on screen but carries no row/column/header structure and linearizes into nonsense for AT ('Monday 2 fried eggs tomato soup garden salad'). The entire relationship lives in the visual alignment of characters. A human must recognize that the ASCII grid encodes a table (with implied row/column headers) or that text is split into parallel columns disrupting reading order; automated tools see a single text node and a syntactically valid <pre

aspectTitle: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
aspectDescription: A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note

aspectTitle: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
aspectDescription: A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note
scenario:
Municipal building-permit 'Scope' section: two stacked yes/no questions — 'Will the work change the building's footprint?' (name=footprint) and 'Is the property in a flood-hazard zone?' (name=flood). Each question is a styled

; each radio pair is labelled Yes/No via
mechanism: All four radios have valid Yes/No accessible names (e086e5 passes). A screen-reader user navigating by form control lands on 'Yes, radio button, 1 of 2' with no programmatic context about which question it answers; both groups announce the same Yes/No and the questions are unassociated paragraphs. Identical option labels across two ungrouped sets create ambiguous group membership — the disambiguator (the stacked prose question) never reaches the accessibility tree.

aspectTitle: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
aspectDescription: A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note
scenario: Arabic (lang=ar, dir=rtl) Health-Ministry new-patient form: a split date-of-birth control with three inputs for اليوم/الشهر/السنة (Day/Month/Year) under a single styled <div> heading تاريخ الميلاد (Date of birth). Each input is named via title='يوم'/'شهر'/'سنة', so no input is unnamed, but there is no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=group+aria-labelledby tying the three inputs to the one question they jointly answer; RTL adds a visual-vs-source ordering wrinkle.
mechanism: Each date input has a non-empty accessible name from title (e086e5 passes). AT encounters three independent fields ('Year, edit text', 'Month...', 'Day...') with no announcement that they compose a single Date of birth value; the unifying question is an unassociated <div> never spoken on entry. The sub-names are ambiguous out of context ('Year' of what?). TT 5.C requires the controls be programmatically associated with their shared question.

aspectTitle: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
aspectDescription: A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note
scenario: Nonprofit donation form built as the deliberate PASS counterpart: it contains the same relationship-bearing structures cases 01-05 get wrong (a radio group with a question, a required cue, a second radio group, a multi-part field) but conveys each programmatically — <fieldset>/<legend> for 'Gift frequency', role=radiogroup+aria-labelledby for 'Designate your gift', aria-required + in-label '(required)' token + aria-describedby for the required note, and role=group+aria-labelledby tying the three phone sub-inputs to 'Daytime phone'.
mechanism: Entering the first radio group, AT announces the legend 'Gift frequency (required)' as the group name; the second group announces 'Designate your gift' via role=radiogroup+aria-labelledby; the required email field announces 'required' via aria-required plus the in-label text token, with its description via aria-describedby; the phone group announces 'Daytime phone (optional), group' with each sub-input tied via aria-describedby. TT 5.C is satisfied: name+description+group associations fully describe each field including the required cue and each group's question.

aspectTitle: Emphasis or special-status meaning conveyed only by visual text variation, with no markup or text equivalent (G117, H49)
aspectDescription: Information is carried solely by a variation in text presentation — bold/italic/underline, a different font face or color, strike-through, larger size — with neither semantic markup (<strong>/<em>/<ins>/<del>) nor an equivalent stated in text. Examples: 'new' or 'on sale' items shown only by bold/red with no '(new)' word; deletions/insertions shown by strike-through/underline with no change list; a glossary term distinguished only by a different font; a warning shown only in red. WCAG explicitly excludes pure color (1.4.1), but bolding/italics/font/strike that convey status, emphasis, or speci
scenario: E-commerce yarn storefront (Shopify Dawn-style grid): three of five products are on sale, signalled ONLY by the product name rendering in bold + one size larger. No '(Sale)' word, no struck original price, no markup, no colour.
mechanism: 'On sale' special status is carried solely by font-weight:700 + larger font-size on the product name; font weight/size are not part of the accessible name or any announced property, so a screen-reader/braille user hears all five names identically and cannot tell which are discounted (F2; G117 not applied).

scenario: Municipal by-law amendment shown as a tracked-changes redline: insertions underlined and deletions struck through using plain CSS-styled <span> elements (text-decoration), with no <ins>/<del>, no change-history list, no inline '(added)/(removed)' text, no colour.
mechanism: Insertion/deletion status is conveyed only by CSS text-decoration: underline/line-through on <span>, which screen readers do not announce (unlike real <del>/<ins>); repealed clause 6.3 and the struck old times read as live policy text, actively misleading the user, and the change relationship is restated in no change-history text (F2; G117's 'change history' example not applied).

WCAG explicitly excludes pure color (1.4.1), but bolding/italics/font/strike that convey status, emphasis, or speci
scenario: B2B Master Services Agreement where 'defined terms' (Service, Term, Confidential Information) are distinguished from ordinary words ONLY by small-caps styling (font-variant-caps: small-caps), with no <dfn>, no link to the definition, no legend stating 'small-caps = defined term', no colour.
mechanism: font-variant-caps:small-caps changes only glyph rendering; the accessible text is identical, so screen readers announce 'service'/'term'/'confidential information' the same whether the occurrence is the load-bearing defined term or the ordinary word — a distinction that materially changes contract scope — and nothing marks the cross-reference to Section 1 (F2; G117 'different font + separate list' not applied).

WCAG explicitly excludes pure color (1.4.1), but bolding/italics/font/strike that convey status, emphasis, or speci
scenario: University LMS course schedule with a structurally exemplary data table (caption, scoped headers, associated cells), where two CANCELLED sessions are signalled ONLY by italic + strike-through cell styling — no 'Cancelled' word, no status column, no <del>/<s>/ARIA, no colour.
mechanism: The 'cancelled' status is carried solely by font-style:italic + text-decoration:line-through on <td>/<th>, which are not announced; a screen-reader/braille user hears the cancelled lab/lecture as a scheduled class and may attend a session that is not running, while the make-up row reads as ordinary. Table semantics are perfect, so this is purely the text-presentation limb of 1.3.1 (F2; G117 not applied).

scenario: Scholarly journal article-listing page where each paper's CORRESPONDING AUTHOR is designated ONLY by their name being bold (font-weight:700 on a <span>), with no '(corresponding author)' text, no asterisk-and-legend, no email/link tied to the name; the intro additionally uses bold decoratively, making the marker ambiguous.
mechanism: The 'corresponding author' relationship is carried solely by font-weight; screen readers announce every author name identically, so the user cannot tell whom to contact for data/materials even though the intro tells them to 'contact the relevant author'. A second decorative bold use makes the convention undiscoverable from the page (F2; G117 not applied).

scenario: BOUNDARY/PASS variant: a product maintenance guide where the one safety-critical step (shut off water before opening housing) is visually emphasised bold+larger — the same risky pattern — BUT uses <strong> markup (H49) AND begins with the literal word 'Important:' in text (G117), so the special status is both programmatically determinable and available in text.
mechanism: The status is conveyed by the word 'Important:' (text equivalent per G117) AND by the <strong> element (programmatically-determinable strong importance per H49), so a screen-reader/braille user gets the warning regardless of styling; the larger font-size is now redundant decoration. Presentation PLUS a text/markup equivalent — 1.3.1 met.
